paras: The mob assault on Pettibone took place in Mobile, Alabama, on a Sunday evening in November 1880, probably November 21, when a large crowd roughly handled a Black man named Pettibone after his arrest and talked of lynching him. He and a second Black man had been arrested, accused of stopping two "young ladies" on the street; no killing was reported, and the episode is known from a single Alabama news brief.

According to the brief, two "young ladies" were stopped on a Mobile street on Sunday evening by two "colored men," one of whom laid his hand on one woman's shoulder while the other put his arm around her companion. The women were said to have struck one man, who fell back into the gutter, and to have hit the other with a brick. Their screams drew "some gentlemen," and both men were arrested.

A "large crowd" then collected, and one of the two men, Pettibone, "was roughly handled" by it, with "talk of lynching him." The brief does not name the arresting party, the street, any injury to Pettibone, or where he was taken afterward.
No report of charges, a hearing, a trial or the later fate of either man appears in the coverage found.

The only account found ran on November 27, 1880, in the Columbus Daily Enquirer-Sun of Georgia, as one item in an "Alabama News" column between notes on a bridge accident and a federal timber-cutting case. The item gave the women's version as fact, identified the men only by race and, for one, a surname, and reported the crowd's rough handling and the lynching talk without comment. No Mobile paper's own account, reprint, editorial or Black-press response was found.
